stem:
You are the emergency registrar. A 62 year old man presents with 4 days of productive cough, fevers, and worsening shortness of breath.

He is a lifelong non smoker with well controlled hypertension. On assessment he sits forward, speaks in short phrases, and has bronchial breath sounds at the right base with dullness to percussion. Extremities are warm and well perfused.

Vital signs: pulse 118, blood pressure 92/64, respiratory rate 32, SpO2 89% in room air, temperature 39.1. Chest x ray shows dense consolidation in the right lower lobe with no pleural effusion. Arterial blood gas on room air: pH 7.44, pCO2 32 mmHg, pO2 62 mmHg, HCO3 24 mmol/L. Serum sodium 132, urea 9.8, albumin 32, pH from arterial sample 7.44.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118, BP 92/64, RR 32, SpO2 89% room air, temperature 39.1
data_table.Examination: Sits forward; speaks in short phrases; right basal bronchial breathing with dullness; warm peripheries
data_table.Investigations: CXR right lower lobe consolidation; no effusion
data_table.Arterial blood gas: pH 7.44; pCO2 32 mmHg; pO2 62 mmHg; HCO3 24 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management pathway based on Australian severity scoring?

options.text: Admit to a high acuity or intensive care bed for intravenous ceftriaxone plus azithromycin and titrated oxygen
options.rationale: SMART-COP components met include systolic BP under 90, multilobar not applicable but albumin under 35, respiratory rate 30 or above, tachycardia 125 or above, and pO2 60 to 70 mmHg on room air; the total predicts need for intensive respiratory or vasopressor support; TG antibiotics are ceftriaxone plus azithromycin (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; Charles et al. SMART-COP validation Clin Infect Dis 2008).

options.text: Discharge on oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily for 5 days with GP review at 48 hours to reassess
options.rationale: Discharge is not appropriate for SMART-COP high risk with hypoxia and hypotension; hospitalisation is mandatory (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Admit to a general medical ward on oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily plus doxycycline 100 mg twice daily
options.rationale: This regimen is TG mild to moderate community acquired pneumonia and does not cover severe pneumonia; a high acuity bed is required (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Commence intravenous piperacillin tazobactam and vancomycin empirically as hospital acquired pneumonia cover
options.rationale: This presentation is community acquired pneumonia rather than hospital acquired; broadening to antipseudomonal cover is not indicated without specific risk factors (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Give oseltamivir 75 mg orally twice daily and hold antibiotics until respiratory viral panel returns
options.rationale: Antibiotic therapy for severe pneumonia is not deferred pending viral panels; consolidation, hypoxia, and toxicity mandate empirical antibiotics now (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: SMART-COP identifies severe community acquired pneumonia. This man meets several criteria (systolic BP under 90, albumin under 35, RR at or above 30, tachycardia at or above 125, pO2 60 to 70 on air), so he needs high acuity or ICU care with intravenous ceftriaxone plus azithromycin and titrated oxygen. Mild to moderate regimens and outpatient care are inappropriate.
key_points: SMART-COP identifies patients needing intensive support.
Severe CAP: intravenous ceftriaxone plus azithromycin.
Do not use hospital acquired regimens or defer for viral results.
explanation.pearls: Severe community acquired pneumonia by SMART-COP is admitted to high acuity or ICU for IV ceftriaxone plus azithromycin; mild to moderate oral regimens do not cover this severity.

sources.label: Charles et al. SMART-COP validation Clin Infect Dis 2008

subtopic_detail: Rapid TIA workup and secondary prevention
stem:
You are the acute stroke registrar. A 68 year old man presents 3 hours after a 25 minute episode of right sided arm weakness and expressive aphasia that has fully resolved. This is his first ever event.

He has hypertension on perindopril 8 mg daily and hyperlipidaemia on atorvastatin 20 mg daily. He is a former smoker who quit 6 years ago. He does not take antiplatelets and has no history of intracranial haemorrhage or major bleeding.

On examination he is fully oriented with normal power, sensation, and speech. Blood pressure is 158/92, pulse 78 regular, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 98% in room air, temperature 36.6. Non contrast CT brain and CT angiogram from arch to vertex show no acute infarct or intracranial haemorrhage and a 50% left internal carotid artery stenosis. Blood glucose is 6.2 mmol/L. ECG shows sinus rhythm.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 158/92, pulse 78 regular, RR 16, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Neurology: Fully resolved right arm weakness and expressive aphasia; no residual deficit
data_table.Imaging: Non contrast CT brain no acute infarct or haemorrhage; CTA arch to vertex 50% left internal carotid artery stenosis
data_table.Other tests: Blood glucose 6.2 mmol/L; ECG sinus rhythm
data_table.Medications: Perindopril 8 mg daily; atorvastatin 20 mg daily; ex smoker; no antiplatelets

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate secondary prevention regimen?

options.text: Commence aspirin 100 mg orally daily alone as monotherapy for lifelong secondary prevention after the event
options.rationale: Aspirin alone in the first 21 days after high risk TIA is inferior to short course DAPT for recurrent stroke prevention as shown by CHANCE and POINT (Source: Stroke Foundation Living Guidelines).

options.text: Load aspirin 300 mg and clopidogrel 300 mg, then aspirin 100 mg daily plus clopidogrel 75 mg daily for 21 days
options.rationale: The Stroke Foundation Australia guideline and CHANCE/POINT trials recommend short course dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) with aspirin plus clopidogrel for 21 days after a high risk TIA (ABCD2 4 or above) or minor stroke without haemorrhage, followed by single antiplatelet (Source: Stroke Foundation Living Guidelines).

options.text: Commence apixaban 5 mg orally twice daily because the TIA is presumed cardioembolic pending Holter monitoring
options.rationale: Anticoagulation is only indicated when atrial fibrillation or another cardioembolic source is documented; ECG is in sinus rhythm and workup has not yet identified one (Source: Stroke Foundation Living Guidelines).

options.text: Refer for urgent carotid endarterectomy today because a 50% carotid stenosis mandates same day surgical repair
options.rationale: Carotid endarterectomy is recommended for symptomatic stenosis 70 to 99% ideally within 2 weeks; 50% is not a mandatory surgical stenosis (Source: Stroke Foundation Living Guidelines).

options.text: Commence intravenous alteplase because he presents within the 4.5 hour window even though symptoms have resolved
options.rationale: Alteplase is for acute ischaemic stroke with a persisting deficit; a fully resolved TIA does not meet the treatment criteria (Source: Stroke Foundation Living Guidelines).

explanation.summary: This is a high risk TIA in a previously untreated patient with no haemorrhage on imaging. Australian guidance uses short course DAPT (aspirin plus clopidogrel) for 21 days followed by single antiplatelet, alongside high intensity statin therapy and BP optimisation. Alteplase is only for persisting deficit. Endarterectomy is for 70 to 99% symptomatic stenosis.
key_points: High risk TIA: aspirin plus clopidogrel for 21 days then single antiplatelet.
Carotid endarterectomy is for 70 to 99% symptomatic stenosis within 2 weeks.
explanation.pearls: After a high risk TIA (ABCD2 4 or above) with no haemorrhage, load aspirin 300 mg and clopidogrel 300 mg then continue both for 21 days before stepping down to single antiplatelet.

stem:
You are the general medicine registrar. A 74 year old woman presents with 6 days of new right sided temporal headache and 2 days of jaw claudication when chewing steak. She denies visual loss, diplopia, or scalp tenderness.

She has a background of osteoporosis on denosumab and hypertension on amlodipine. She takes no anticoagulants and has no allergies.

On examination the right temporal artery is prominent and tender but pulsatile. Visual acuity is 6/6 bilaterally. Fundoscopy shows a normal disc bilaterally with no pallor. Cranial nerves are otherwise intact.

Vital signs are within normal limits. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate 84 mm/hour (0-30), C reactive protein 92 mg/L (0-5), platelets 445, ALP 148 U/L (30-120).

data_table.Symptoms: 6 days right temporal headache; 2 days jaw claudication on chewing; no visual loss or diplopia; no scalp tenderness reported
data_table.Examination: Right temporal artery prominent and tender but pulsatile; visual acuity 6/6 bilaterally; fundoscopy normal discs
data_table.Inflammatory markers: ESR 84 mm/hour (0-30); CRP 92 mg/L (0-5); platelets 445 x10^9/L
data_table.Liver panel: ALP 148 U/L (30-120); other LFTs within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Commence intravenous methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 3 days for anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy prophylaxis
options.rationale: Pulse methylprednisolone is reserved for GCA with visual involvement or ischaemic complications, not for uncomplicated presentations (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association GCA guidance).

options.text: Await temporal artery biopsy results before starting corticosteroids to avoid masking pathology
options.rationale: Delaying steroids risks irreversible visual loss and biopsy remains diagnostic despite up to 2 weeks of treatment (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association GCA guidance).

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone 60 mg orally daily immediately and arrange a temporal artery biopsy within 14 days
options.rationale: Australian and BSR guidance start prednisolone 40 to 60 mg daily immediately for suspected GCA and biopsy within 1 to 2 weeks; steroids should not be delayed pending biopsy because temporal biopsy findings persist for weeks (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association GCA guidance; BSR GCA guideline 2020).

options.text: Commence tocilizumab 162 mg subcutaneous weekly as monotherapy for steroid sparing induction
options.rationale: Tocilizumab is a steroid sparing adjunct in relapsing GCA, not a monotherapy induction agent (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association GCA guidance).

options.text: Commence naproxen 500 mg twice daily and reassess in 48 hours after inflammatory markers repeat
options.rationale: NSAIDs are not adequate treatment for GCA and delay effective immunosuppression while irreversible visual loss can occur (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association GCA guidance).

explanation.summary: New temporal headache with jaw claudication and grossly elevated ESR and CRP in a woman over 50 is GCA until proven otherwise. Start prednisolone 40 to 60 mg daily immediately and arrange temporal artery biopsy within 14 days; do not delay steroids. Pulse methylprednisolone is reserved for visual involvement or ischaemic complications.
key_points: Start prednisolone 40 to 60 mg daily now.
Temporal artery biopsy within 14 days; positivity persists on treatment.
Reserve pulse methylprednisolone for visual or ischaemic involvement.
explanation.pearls: In suspected GCA start prednisolone 40 to 60 mg daily immediately and biopsy within 14 days; visual complications escalate to pulse methylprednisolone.

sources.label: BSR Guideline for the diagnosis and treatment of giant cell arteritis 2020

stem:
You are the oncology inpatient registrar. A 61 year old woman with locally advanced gastric adenocarcinoma on cycle 3 of FLOT chemotherapy is admitted with new left leg swelling. Compression ultrasound confirms an occlusive left femoral vein deep venous thrombosis without extension into the iliac veins. She is haemodynamically stable and has no chest symptoms.

She has no history of bleeding, no varices, and no active peptic ulceration on recent gastroscopy. Recent bloods: haemoglobin 108 g/L (115-165), platelets 168, creatinine 68 micromol/L. Her medications include ondansetron 8 mg TDS during chemotherapy cycles and pantoprazole 40 mg daily.

There is no mucosal bleeding on examination. She is fully oriented and mobilising.

data_table.Imaging: Left femoral vein occlusive DVT on compression ultrasound; no iliac extension; no PE symptoms
data_table.Malignancy: Locally advanced gastric adenocarcinoma; cycle 3 FLOT chemotherapy
data_table.Bleeding history: No prior bleeding; no varices; no active peptic ulceration on recent gastroscopy
data_table.Bloods: Haemoglobin 108 g/L (115-165); platelets 168 x10^9/L; creatinine 68 micromol/L
data_table.Medications: Ondansetron 8 mg TDS; pantoprazole 40 mg daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate anticoagulant regimen?

options.text: Aspirin 100 mg orally daily and knee high compression stockings for at least 3 months without anticoagulant
options.rationale: Aspirin is not adequate acute anticoagulation for a proximal DVT in cancer; it is reserved for extended prophylaxis in specific low risk contexts (Source: TSANZ Australian VTE Guidelines).

options.text: Rivaroxaban 15 mg orally twice daily for 21 days then 20 mg daily for at least 6 months of active cancer
options.rationale: Rivaroxaban is associated with a higher major GI bleeding signal in gastrointestinal malignancy than apixaban and is not preferred in gastric cancer (Source: TSANZ Australian VTE Guidelines).

options.text: Warfarin bridging with enoxaparin 1 mg/kg twice daily until INR 2 to 3 for a minimum of 3 months
options.rationale: Warfarin is inferior to LMWH and DOACs in active cancer because of drug interactions with chemotherapy and unstable INR from vomiting or nutritional swings (Source: TSANZ Australian VTE Guidelines).

options.text: Apixaban 10 mg orally twice daily for 7 days then 5 mg twice daily for at least 6 months of active cancer
options.rationale: Australian and international cancer VTE guidance now supports DOACs (apixaban or rivaroxaban) over LMWH for most patients without upper GI or genitourinary tumours; gastric cancer requires case by case review given bleeding risk, but apixaban is preferred over rivaroxaban in gastric or GI cancers because of a lower luminal bleeding signal (Source: TSANZ Australian VTE Guidelines; Caravaggio and SELECT-D trials).

options.text: Retrievable inferior vena cava filter alone instead of anticoagulation because of chemotherapy bleeding risk
options.rationale: IVC filters are reserved for absolute contraindication to anticoagulation; she has no active bleeding and her platelets are 168, so anticoagulation is preferred (Source: TSANZ Australian VTE Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Cancer associated VTE now typically uses apixaban or rivaroxaban over LMWH. In gastric or other luminal GI cancers apixaban is preferred because of a lower luminal bleeding signal than rivaroxaban. Continue for at least 6 months and while cancer or chemotherapy remains active.
key_points: DOAC over LMWH for most cancer VTE.
Apixaban preferred in luminal GI cancers.
Duration at least 6 months and while active cancer.
explanation.pearls: For DVT in gastric or other luminal GI cancer, apixaban is preferred over rivaroxaban because of a lower major GI bleeding signal in the Caravaggio and SELECT-D data.

sources.label: SELECT-D trial (Young et al. J Clin Oncol 2018)

subtopic_detail: Adrenal crisis in steroid dependent patient
stem:
You are the medical registrar on for after hours. A 54 year old woman with long standing rheumatoid arthritis on prednisolone 7.5 mg daily for 6 years presents with 24 hours of fever, watery diarrhoea, and vomiting.

She has not taken any prednisolone today because she cannot keep tablets down. She has no other medications and no allergies.

On assessment she is drowsy and cool peripherally. Peripheries are cool with capillary refill of 4 seconds centrally.

Vital signs: pulse 128, blood pressure 82/54, respiratory rate 24, SpO2 98% in room air, temperature 39.0. Point of care glucose 3.1 mmol/L. Bloods: sodium 128, potassium 5.4 mmol/L, urea 12 mmol/L, creatinine 132 micromol/L. Venous blood gas shows pH 7.30, HCO3 18, lactate 3.0 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128, BP 82/54, RR 24, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 39.0
data_table.Examination: Drowsy; cool peripheries; capillary refill 4 seconds
data_table.Electrolytes: Sodium 128 mmol/L; potassium 5.4 mmol/L; urea 12; creatinine 132 micromol/L
data_table.Medication history: Prednisolone 7.5 mg daily for 6 years; missed today because of vomiting

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.text: Commence noradrenaline infusion targeted to a MAP of 65 mmHg and defer corticosteroid until inotrope is titrated
options.rationale: Corticosteroid replacement is definitive in adrenal crisis and must not be delayed while titrating vasopressors; inotropes remain refractory without steroid (Source: ESA Adrenal Insufficiency Guideline).

options.text: Restart oral prednisolone at double her usual daily dose once she stops vomiting and rehydrate her with oral fluids
options.rationale: Oral therapy is unreliable in vomiting shocked patients; parenteral hydrocortisone is required for adrenal crisis (Source: ESA Adrenal Insufficiency Guideline).

options.text: Give intravenous dexamethasone 8 mg once alongside 0.9% saline resuscitation and await the results of a short synacthen test
options.rationale: Dexamethasone lacks mineralocorticoid activity needed in adrenal crisis; deferring hydrocortisone for a synacthen test delays life saving treatment (Source: ESA Adrenal Insufficiency Guideline).

options.text: Give intravenous fludrocortisone 100 microgram alone with 0.9% saline resuscitation and reassess in 4 hours
options.rationale: Fludrocortisone is not available in a parenteral form suitable for crisis and does not replace hydrocortisone in acute adrenal insufficiency (Source: ESA Adrenal Insufficiency Guideline).

options.text: IV hydrocortisone 100 mg immediately then 200 mg over 24 hours by infusion, plus 0.9% saline and 10% dextrose
options.rationale: This is an adrenal crisis in a chronically suppressed patient; the Endocrine Society of Australia recommends hydrocortisone 100 mg IV bolus then 200 mg per 24 hours by infusion with fluid resuscitation and glucose correction (Source: ESA Adrenal Insufficiency Guideline; Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

explanation.summary: Chronic prednisolone therapy suppresses the hypothalamic pituitary adrenal axis and an intercurrent illness with vomiting can precipitate an adrenal crisis. Treatment is intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus then 200 mg per 24 hours, 0.9% saline resuscitation, and glucose replacement. Dexamethasone lacks mineralocorticoid effect and should not replace hydrocortisone in crisis.
key_points: IV hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus then 200 mg per 24 hours.
Fluid resuscitate with 0.9% saline; correct hypoglycaemia with 10% dextrose.
Do not use dexamethasone as substitute; do not defer for synacthen test.
explanation.pearls: In adrenal crisis give IV hydrocortisone 100 mg then 200 mg per 24 hours by infusion; dexamethasone lacks mineralocorticoid activity and is not the substitute of choice.
